books.section: Topic 4.5 Market Revolution: Economic Transformations, B. Advances in Technology

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.5 B, and Princeton Review, Chapter 8: Eli Whitney, who had earlier developed the cotton gin, proposed making musket parts to exact specifications so that any part would fit any musket. He showed the idea to Thomas Jefferson and James Madison by taking apart several rifles, mixing the parts, and rebuilding the rifles from whatever parts he picked up. Makers of clocks, watches, tools, and farm implements soon used the same method.
stimulus.source_note: Secondary text: paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.5 B, and Princeton Review, Chapter 8. Paraphrased, not quoted.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The spread of the method in the passage to clocks, watches, tools, and farm implements best shows that

options.text: Whitney himself founded the clock and tool industries
options.misconception: Whitney worked on muskets and cotton; other makers applied his method to clocks, tools, and implements.

options.text: standardized parts became a general base for mass production
the cotton gin and the musket were the same invention
options.misconception: The gin cleaned cotton and the musket method standardized parts; they are two different inventions by one man.

options.text: American factories stopped making textiles after 1800
options.misconception: Textiles were the leading early factory industry and kept growing; the method spread to new industries as well.

rationales.A: The passage says other makers used the method. Whitney showed the idea; the clock, tool, and implement makers adopted it.
rationales.B: Once parts were standard, the same approach worked for any machine. That is why it spread from guns to clocks, tools, and farm implements.
rationales.C: Whitney invented both the gin and the parts method, but they solve different problems: cleaning cotton and fitting parts.
rationales.D: Textile mills were the first great factory industry and they grew through this whole period. The method added industries, not replaced textiles.
rationales.general:
1. List where the method went. From muskets it spread to clocks, watches, tools, and farm implements.
2. Ask what those goods share. All are machines built from many parts.
3. Put it together. A method that works for any machine is a general base for making goods in quantity.
Background: Interchangeable parts gave birth to the machine-tool industry, which built specialized machines for textiles and transport.
Remember: when an idea jumps from one industry to many, it has become a general method, not a single trick.
